prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All my life I was face to face with her, at meal-times, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. You could have asked, then, for information about her? There was a room apart she kept herself in, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my reflection. I learned from her even so. Walking her shore I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers I found her garden had forestalled me in providing civilities for my desk. ‘Tell me about life,’ I would say, ‘you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.’ Her eyes had a fine shame, remembering her privacy being invaded from further off than she expected. ‘Do you think death is the end?’ frivolously I would ask her. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip down, and how the upper remained firm, reticent as the bud that is the precursor of the flower.

Because the original piece is deeply poetic and literary (written in the style of reflective memoir), "professional" in this context means **refined, grammatically flawless, and elevated in cadence**, rather than corporate.

### Option 1: High Literary & Eloquent (Recommended)
*This version preserves the poetic cadence, imagery, and emotional depth of the original while smoothing out awkward phrasing and enhancing the flow.*

> Throughout my life, I found myself face-to-face with her—at mealtimes, beside the hearth, and even within the deepest intimacies of our shared bed. Might one have expected me, then, to offer a true account of who she was? Yet she held a private sanctuary within herself, tantalizing me by leading me to its glass door, only to leave me confronting my own reflection. 
> 
> Even so, I learned from her. Wandering her shores, I discovered treasures cast up from her depths that spoke to me of a different order—devout worshipper of untamed nature though I was. She drew her riches from the storehouse of art: fragments of antique lace, delicate as frost; porcelain from a forgotten era; a purse far more precious than anything it could contain. Returning from the fields with an offering of wildflowers, I would find her garden had already forestalled me, adorning my desk with its own cultivated graces.
> 
> “Tell me about life,” I would say to her, “you who served as its harbinger in the delivery of our child.” Her eyes held a subtle shade of shame, recalling how her privacy had been breached from a distance far greater than she had anticipated.
> 
> “Do you think death is the end?” I would ask her, perhaps too lightly. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival—wrenching her lower lip downward while the upper remained firm and unyielding, as reticent as a bud preceding the flower.

*This version focuses on crispness, clarity, and subtle elegance while keeping every detail intact.*

outputs.L2:
Throughout our shared existence, she was constantly at my side—during daily meals, beside the warm hearth, and within the deepest physical closeness of our bed. Yet, if anyone had asked me to describe her true self, could I have actually answered? A private sanctuary existed within her; she would mischievously guide me to its clear glass entrance, only to force me to look at my own reflected image rather than her inner world. 

Even so, she served as my teacher. Though I personally revered untamed, wild nature, wandering along the edges of her personality brought me face-to-face with remnants cast up from her deep interior, hinting at a far more refined reality. Her treasures belonged to the world of artistic craft: antique lace as delicate as winter frost, porcelain from an earlier era, and a coin pouch whose intrinsic worth eclipsed anything placed inside it. When I would trek back from the open fields to offer her wildflowers, I would discover that blooms from her own cultivated garden had already beat me to the task, adorning my desk with elegance.

"Explain existence to me," I would ask her, "for you were the conduit that brought our baby into this world." Hearing this, her gaze would fill with a subtle modesty as she remembered how a force from much farther away than she ever anticipated had intruded upon her intimate realm.

In a lighthearted manner, I used to inquire, "Do you believe everything terminates with death?" Looking back now, I recall the suddenness of her passing—how it yanked her bottom lip downward, while her top lip stayed composed and tight, remaining as closed and silent as a flower's unexpanded bud.
outputs.L3:
Despite the profound intimacy of our shared life—the quiet mornings, the unspoken routines, and the physical closeness of living side-by-side—her inner world remained tantalizingly elusive. She moved through our days wrapped in a soft, impenetrable veil of privacy. I knew the cadence of her breath and the rhythm of her footsteps, yet the deepest currents of her thoughts were a sanctuary to which she alone held the key. 

We were a study in contrasts. Left to my own devices, I gravitated toward the raw, untamed elements of wild nature, finding comfort in unpolished wilderness and rugged landscapes. She, however, gently expanded my horizons, opening my eyes to the elegance of art and the rich tapestry of human history. She possessed a quiet refinement that seeped into everything she touched. Long before I would think to bring order or beauty to a room, she would subtly transform it. My own workspace, often a chaos of solitary thought, would be quietly enriched by her hand—a chosen object, a flower, a rearrangement of light—bringing grace and civility into the very fabric of my daily routine.

This quiet strength reached its zenith when she became the messenger of life, bearing our child into the world. It was a miraculous transformation, yet I could not shake a poignant realization: the visceral, public nature of childbirth felt like an unwitting invasion of her profound privacy. To bring forth life required an exposure that ran counter to her self-contained essence, making her sacrifice feel all the more sacred and heavy.

That deep-seated guard was something she defended fiercely, particularly against the ultimate unknown. On the rare occasions when the topic of mortality surfaced in our conversations, I would catch a swift, fleeting flicker of raw emotion in her eyes—a flash of sorrow or fear—immediately followed by a firm, stoic reticence. She would close the door on the subject as quickly as it had opened, choosing to face the vast expanse of existence with a quiet, unwavering silence that I came to deeply respect, even if I could never fully cross its threshold.
outputs.L4:
I was a man forged from coarser elements—loud-footed, impatient, and governed by the restless, violent impulses of a world that demands to be conquered. She, by contrast, seemed to have arrived from a quieter realm, one governed by restraint and delicate cadences. For nearly fifty years, I shared a roof with her, ate at her table, and slept in the warm hollow beside her, yet I spent that entire lifetime feeling like an intruder standing at the threshold of a sanctuary.

To know her was an exercise in patient observation. I watched the way she moved through our house, leaving almost no trace of her passage, like a shadow gliding across polished wood. Her world was one of meticulous, quiet refinements. In the early afternoons, she would sit by the bay window with her watercolors, capturing the fleeting geometries of falling leaves or the translucent veins of a beetle’s wing. Her brushwork was economical, precise, and hauntingly beautiful. I often sat across from her, pretending to read, searching her face for the hidden source of that artistic composure. What thoughts occupied the spaces between her gentle breaths? What griefs or joys had she locked away in the quiet vaults of her mind? 

Whenever I tried to press beyond her borders—to demand, with my clumsy, untamed curiosity, a total surrender of her secrets—she would offer a soft, impenetrable smile. It was not a wall intended to exclude me, but rather a boundary of self-possession that she refused to violate. She listened to my bluster, my existential anxieties, and my loud, unformed opinions with a grave and generous patience. Where I brought chaos, noise, and dirt into the house, she responded with symmetry, soft music, and a poise that gradually, imperceptibly, smoothed my roughest edges. Without ever issuing a command or a reproach, her mere presence civilized me. She taught my heavy hands how to hold fragile things.

Yet, I always believed that one day the mask of her composure would slip. I harbored a selfish, desperate desire to see her unmoored, if only to prove that she was made of the same fragile, frightened clay as the rest of us. 

That test came in the autumn of our twilight years, when the illness took hold of her body. 

As the disease stripped away her physical strength, I waited for the panic, the anger, or the bitter despair that I knew would have consumed me in her place. But it never came. In the face of her own mortality, her guarded inner world did not fracture; it solidified into something profound and luminous. She met pain with the same quiet dignity she had brought to her art, arranging her bedsheets with trembling hands, sipping her tea with deliberate grace, and looking out the window at the encroaching winter with an unshakeable calm. 

In her final days, as I sat weeping beside her, clutching her frail hand with all the desperate violence of my untamed nature, she looked at me with clear, unclouded eyes. Even death, the great undoer of human pride, could not rob her of her mystery or her majesty. 

It was only then, in the absolute quiet that followed her final breath, that I truly understood. Her mystery was not a puzzle meant to be solved, nor a secret meant to be revealed. It was her sanctuary—a stoic, inviolable core of selfhood that had sustained her through life and elevated her in death. She had left me behind in a world that felt suddenly larger, harsher, and far too loud, but the light of her civilizing grace remained, etched forever into the quietest corners of my soul.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary reflection by a widower capturing the elusive, mysterious nature of his late wife and the quiet distance that existed between them despite a lifetime of intimacy.
counterfactuals.output:
We spent forty years in the intimate geometry of a shared life. We knew the precise cadence of each other’s footfalls on the stairs, the exact temperature of tea the other preferred, the unspoken vocabulary of a glance across a crowded room. We slept beneath the same heavy quilt, our breaths aligning in the dark like twin pendulums. 

Yet, even now, months after her hospice bed was cleared away, Eleanor remains an evening light I could never quite catch in my hands. 

There was always a quiet coast in her that I was not permitted to land upon. It was not a coldness—she loved me with a fierce, steady grace—but rather a profound, unyielding interiority. I would catch her sitting by the window in the late afternoon, her teacup resting cold in her lap, staring out into the garden with an expression so vast and terrible in its tranquility that I felt like a trespasser in my own hallway. When I asked what she was thinking, she would turn, offer me a small, pale smile, and say, "Nothing, my dear. Just watching the crows."

I spent decades believing that time would dissolve that thin, impenetrable pane of glass between us. I thought intimacy was a process of total erosion, that eventually, two people would spill completely into one another until no secrets remained. But Eleanor preserved her wilderness. She kept her childhood memories sealed like pressed flowers in a forgotten book; she kept her griefs folded neatly in drawers I never opened. 

Now, moving through this silent house, surrounded by her half-filled crossword puzzles and the lingering scent of her lavender soap, I realize that the distance between us was not a failure of our marriage, but its very architecture. She was a sea I learned to navigate without ever needing to measure its depths.

I used to think that to love someone fully was to know them completely. But standing here in the blue dusk of our bedroom, folding a scarf she left over the back of a chair, I know better. Love was not the conquest of her mysteries. It was the willingness to stand at the threshold of her solitude, year after year, and simply keep watch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic prose piece about a man who worships untamed nature reflecting on his wife, a woman of quiet artifice and culture. Mention her private room, her antique treasures, and a poignant memory of her final moments.
counterfactuals.output:
I have spent my life kneeling before the altar of the untamed. My gods are the hemlocks that split granite, the indifference of winter gales, and the raw, iron smell of wet earth after a thaw. I am a man built of rough edges and weathered marrow, accustomed to a world that breathes without permission.

And yet, I surrendered my heart to a woman who lived in measure and cadence, a creature of exquisite artifice. 

Where I saw beauty in the rot and rebirth of the forest floor, Clara found it in the deliberate, the preserved, the cultivated. She was a song written in a quiet room while I was the howl outside the glass.

Now, I walk into her sanctuary, pushing open the heavy mahogany door that still holds her scent—warm amber, pressed iris, and old paper. This was her private domain, a quiet kingdom where the wilderness was strictly forbidden to cross the threshold. Here, the chaos of the world was hushed by thick damask curtains that turned the wild afternoon sun into a soft, honeyed dusk.

I stand clumsy in my heavy boots among her treasures. Clara did not just collect objects; she curated time itself. On her rosewood desk sits a silver-backed hand mirror from some long-forgotten century, its glass slightly clouded like a frozen pond. Beside it rest fragile teacups of eggshell porcelain, painted with gilded birds that would never fly, and a brass astrolabe that measured stars she preferred to view through a telescope rather than under an open, freezing sky. 

She believed in the elegance of human hands over the violence of nature. She believed that to carve, to weave, to paint, and to polish was a sacred rebellion against the dark. I used to laugh—gently, always gently—at her little ivory boxes and her lace collars, asking how she could care for things so easily broken. 

*“Because they require us to be careful, my love,”* she had whispered once, her fingers tracing the carved curve of an antique cameo. *“The mountain will endure your stomping. But this asks for your grace.”*

In the end, it was her grace that broke me. 

My mind pulls me back to that final autumn evening, to the memory that remains pinned to my chest like a thorn. The wild outside her window was performing its brutal, beautiful theater—a storm was stripping the oak trees bare, hurling leaves against the glass in a frenzy of bronze and crimson. I wanted to open the window, to let the cool, rain-washed air in, to offer her the primordial strength of the earth I so worshipped. 

But Clara, pale and diminished against the high feather pillows, turned her weak head away from the window. She did not want the storm. 

With trembling, translucent fingers, she reached out to her nightstand. She did not grab my calloused hand first; she reached for her small, silver-stoppered vial of lavender water. With an effort that seemed to cost her the last of her breath, she dabbed a drop onto her wrists, pressing them together in a quiet, instinctual ritual of dignity. Then, she smoothed the edge of her embroidered silk sheet, ensuring even in her undoing that the lines were straight, the presentation serene. 

Only then did she look at me. Only then did she take my hand.

*"Do not let the moss take me too quickly,"* she murmured, her voice a thread of gossamer. *"Keep me tidy for a little while."*

She closed her eyes as the tempest outside reached its crescendo, departing not like a fallen tree in a forest, but like a candle extinguished by a soft, deliberate breath. 

Now, I sit in her velvet armchair, a wild beast harboring a fragile grief. Outside, the forest calls to me—the pines sway, the river rises, the dirt waits. But for today, I remain inside her quiet room. I touch the cool silver of her mirror, wind the tiny brass gears of her antique clock, and learn the slow, heartbreaking worship of things made to be cherished, and lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In the introspective, lyrical style of mid-20th-century British prose, write a short monologue exploring how a husband learns about art and life through his enigmatic spouse, touching on the birth of their child and her stoic reaction to death.
counterfactuals.output:
Before I met Eleanor, I lived, as men of my station so often do, entirely in the foreground of things. A chair was merely oak and upholstery; a painting, a clever arrangement of pigment intended to cover a patch of bare wallpaper. I was content with the simple draughtsmanship of existence, utterly blind to its light and shadow.

It was Eleanor who taught me how to see. I remember standing beside her during our early days, in the chill, gray hush of the Tate, before a landscape by Turner. Where I saw only a blur of yellow and storm-cloud, Eleanor saw the precise moment at which beauty and terror collide. "Notice how the light doesn't conquer the dark, Richard," she whispered in that quiet, measured cadence of hers. "It merely makes the dark bearable." In that instant, the scales fell away. Through her eyes, I began to understand that art was not an ornament to life, but its most ruthless, honest translation. Life itself, she demonstrated without ever giving a lecture, demanded an exacting, courageous attention.

When our child was born—on a bitter Tuesday in November, with the rain knocking against the windowpanes like fine gravel—I had prepared myself for a tumult of sentiment. I anticipated tears, or the feverish, triumphant joy one reads of in novels. But Eleanor, exhausted and pale against the damp linen, held the infant with an expression of profound, almost severe solemnity. She did not weep. She looked down at that small, crumpled face as though receiving a long-expected stranger whose arrival brought both immense grace and a heavy, quiet responsibility. She understood, far sooner than I, that to bring a life into the world is to sign an unwritten treaty with frailty.

And when death came—first for her brother in that senseless, sudden summer, and later taking the quiet warmth from our own hearth—she did not unspool. I had readied myself to be her anchor, to offer the clumsy, comforting platitudes of my upbringing. Yet it was I who faltered in the cold parlor. Eleanor merely walked to the bedside, smoothed the white sheet with a hand that did not tremble, and stood in long, motionless contemplation. She did not rail against the silence; she inhabited it. For Eleanor, death was not a betrayal of life, but its natural, quiet frame—the dark border that gives the painting its form. 

She remains, even now, a citadel I am still learning to explore. Through her, I have learned that we do not possess the light, nor the child, nor the fleeting days we are given; we are merely permitted to observe them, to hold them against the dark for a little while, provided we have the courage not to look away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose poem exploring the contrast between wild nature and refined art within a marriage. Describe a partner who remains an enigma behind a metaphoric glass door, and conclude with a striking visual memory of her lip at the moment of death.
counterfactuals.output:
Our marriage was an elegant gallery constructed over an unmapped marsh. I was the conservator, obsessed with symmetry—with the curated silences of chamber music, the gilding on heavy frames, and the promise that art could keep the world from fraying. But she was the wilderness that refused the canvas. Beneath her tailored linens, she carried the scent of crushed fern and ozone, her quiet moments heavy with the damp, electric stillness that precedes a gale. 

For decades she lived beside me, yet she remained an enigma forever pacing behind a seamless glass door. I could observe her with excruciating clarity—the way she moved through our rooms with the deliberate grace of a Renaissance sketch, even as her gaze strayed toward the storm outside like a captive hawk. I reached for her daily, but my fingers met only the cool, impenetrable pane of her reserve, catching only my own reflection superimposed over her wild, unreachable heart. She was a landscape visible in every detail, yet entirely untouchable, sealed within her own sovereign weather.

And when the end arrived, the refined artifice of our life dissolved into raw, elemental nature. In that quiet room, her breathing slowed to the primitive, uneven tide of a retreating sea, pulling her further past the glass than I could ever follow. What abides now is not the memory of our polished rooms or her quiet restraint, but the striking, solitary image of her lower lip in the exact instant the pulse abandoned it—drained of color to the pale violet of winter slate, yet parted slightly, marked by a single, glistening bead of dark blood where her own teeth had caught the flesh: a fierce, unpolished seed pressed forever into the marble of her death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a passage from a novel where an elderly man remembers his deceased wife, focusing on the philosophical questions he used to ask her about life and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
The steam rising from Arthur’s tea was the only thing moving in the quiet of the parlor, a pale ribbon dissolving into the amber dusk. Opposite him sat the velvet wingback chair, empty now for three years, its fabric still bearing the faint, imagined scent of lavender and old paper.

He had always been the restless one, cursed with a brain that picked at the seams of existence like a loose thread. Clara, by contrast, had been anchored to the earth, grounded by a quiet, immovable serenity. 

He remembered one autumn evening decades ago, when the light had looked precisely like this—thin, golden, and fleeting. She had been sitting in that very chair, paring an apple with a small silver knife, the red skin curling off in one unbroken spiral. 

"Clara," he had asked, leaning forward with the solemn urgency of a young man who believed everything could be solved through debate, "do you think we are built to be finished, or merely interrupted?"

She hadn't looked up immediately. She had preferred to let his questions settle, like dust in a shaft of sunlight, before offering a response. "Interrupted by what, Arthur?"

"By death, of course," he had said, pacing the rug. "If consciousness is the universe trying to understand itself, isn’t it a tragic design that the understanding is cut short just as it begins to mature? Why give us the capacity to love so infinitely, only to bind us to a finite clock? It feels like an error in the architecture."

Clara had sliced a pale wedge of the apple, offering it to him on the flat edge of her blade. "You spend so much time analyzing the house, Arthur, that you forget to live in the rooms."

"That’s not an answer, Clara."

"It’s the only answer there is," she had replied softly, her dark eyes reflecting the lamp light. "A song isn’t a tragedy because it ends. The silence after the last note isn't an error—it’s just where the music lands."

He took the apple wedge then, silenced, as he so often was, by her refusal to be frightened by his abysses. 

Over forty years, he had peppered her with his existential terrors. He had asked her if love was merely a chemical trick to ensure survival, or a literal force, like gravity, that lingered in the ether after the body dissolved. He had asked her if memory was a merciful gift or a cruelty designed to make old age unbearable. 

*If a life is just a sequence of vanishing moments,* he had posited on a dark night when the rain drummed against the glass, *what actually holds us together? What stops us from spilling out into nothingness?*

And Clara, wrapping her hand around his trembling fingers in the dark, had whispered, "I hold you together. And you hold me. The rest is just weather."

Now, sitting alone in the gathering night, Arthur rested his spotted hands on his knees. The room had grown cold. He realized the bitter, beautiful irony of his youth: he had spent decades treating mortality as a grand, philosophical puzzle to be solved, a debate to be won across a tea table. 

He didn't care about the architecture of the universe anymore. He didn't care if the soul was gravity or chemistry, or whether the silence at the end was part of the music. 

He stared at the empty velvet chair, the dark creeping in around its edges, and asked the air the only question that mattered now—the one he had never thought to ask her when she was there to answer.

*How do I bear the music after the song has stopped?*

There was no reply, of course. Only the quiet settling of the house, and the faint, persistent memory of her hand in his, holding him together against the weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
